of the paths and circles placed in such a way that they influence those who watch at a certain time. Thus, ships seem to stand still even when they sail with full sails. Someone will one day demonstrate in which parts of the heavens comets wander, how great they are, and what sort they are, since they go so far removed from the others. We are content with what has been discovered; may posterity also contribute something to the truth. They say that we do not see things beyond through the stars, but that we send our sight through comets. First, if that happens, it does not happen in the part where the star itself is composed of dense and solid fire, but where a rare splendor escapes and scatters into hairs. You see through the intervals of the fires, not through the fires themselves. They say that all stars are round, but comets are elongated, from which it appears they are not stars. But who will grant you that comets are long, when their nature, like that of the others, is in fact a sphere? The brightness is extended just as the sun sends its rays far and wide. The form of the comet itself is one thing, and the light that flows from it is another. Thus, the body of the comets is rounded. However, the splendor appears longer than that of the other heavenly bodies. Why, you ask? Tell me first why the moon receives light so unlike the sun, when it receives it from the sun? Why does it sometimes redden, sometimes grow pale? Why does it have a livid and black color when it is excluded from the view of the sun? Tell me why all the stars have a face in some way dissimilar to each other, and very different from the sun. Just as nothing prevents them from being stars, even if they are not similar, so nothing prevents comets from being eternal and of the same lot as the rest, even if they do not have a similar face. Furthermore, if you consider the world itself, is it not composed of diverse things? Why is it that the sun always burns in Leo and scorches the lands with heat, but in Aquarius it binds the winter and closes the rivers with ice? And yet this star and that one are of the same condition <margin>† rises</margin> even though they are dissimilar in effect and nature. Within a very short time, Aries † rises, and Libra sets most slowly; yet this star and that one are of the same nature, even though the former rises in a short time and the latter is prolonged for a long time. Do you not see how contrary the elements are to one another? There are heavy and light, cold and hot, moist and dry. The whole harmony of this world consists of discord. You deny that a comet is a star because its form does not correspond to the model, nor is it similar to the others. For you see, it is very similar to that one which returns to its place in the thirtieth year, to this one which revisits its seat within a year. Nature does not provide its work according to one form, but prides itself on variety. It made some things more sluggish, others swifter than the rest. It made some things stronger, others more temperate; moreover, it brought some out from the crowd so that they might proceed individually and visibly, and it sent others into a flock. He who thinks that nature is not allowed to do anything except what it does most often is ignorant of its power. It does not show comets frequently; it assigns them another place, other times, and motions unlike the rest. It wished to honor the greatness of its work through these, whose appearance is too beautiful to be considered accidental, whether you consider their size or their brightness, which is greater and more fiery than the others. Indeed, its appearance has something distinguished and unique, not cast into a narrow space and constricted, but released more freely, and embracing the region of many stars. Aristotle says that comets signify a storm and intemperance of winds and rains. What then? Do you not judge it to be a star because it foretells future events? For it is not a sign of a storm in the same way that oil sparking or mold growing into mushrooms is a sign of future rain, or how it is an indication of a raging sea if marine coots play on dry land and desert the known marshes, or a heron flies above the high cloud. But it is a sign in the way the equinox is a sign of heat and cold in the turning year. It is like the things the Chaldeans sing of, concerning what a star determines for the newborn, whether sad or happy. So that you may know this is so, a comet that has just risen does not threaten winds and rains, as Aristotle says, but <margin>The rising of a comet makes the whole year suspect.</margin> it makes the whole year suspect. From this it appears that it did not draw the signs it gives for the near future from what is near, but that it has them stored and compressed by the laws of the world. That comet which appeared when Patruculus and Vopiscus were consuls performed the things that were predicted by Aristotle and Theophrastus. For there were very great and continuous storms everywhere. But in Achaia and Macedonia, cities were destroyed by earthquakes. Their slowness, he says, is an argument that they are heavier and have much of the earthly in themselves. Furthermore, their courses are almost compelled into the cardinal points. Both are false. I will speak about the former first, because things that are carried more slowly are heavy. What then? Is the star of Saturn, which completes its journey the most slowly of all, heavy? And yet it has an argument for lightness in that it is above the others. But, you say, it travels in a larger orbit,

<summary>Seneca argues for the celestial and eternal nature of comets, rejecting the idea that their unique appearance or irregular movement excludes them from being stars, and dismissing the view that they are merely atmospheric phenomena.</summary>
